quickAnswer.question: How do I convert a voicemail to text?
quickAnswer.answer: Save the voicemail as an audio file (on iPhone: open the message, tap Share, then Save to Files), and upload it to TranscriptX. It transcribes the whole message into text in seconds, in over 100 languages, ready to read, copy, edit or download. It's free to use every day, with no app and no sign-up.

content: Voicemail to text turns a spoken voicemail into written words, so you can read a message instead of dialling in and listening to it, often twice to catch a phone number.

Your phone may already do a version of this. iPhone shows a transcription under each voicemail and, with Live Voicemail, while the caller is still speaking. Phone by Google and Google Voice show transcripts too. Those previews are free and automatic, and for a quick look at who called they are often all you need.

They also have limits. They depend on your carrier, region and phone language, they cover a short list of languages, and they can come back cut off or not at all. TranscriptX works on the voicemail audio itself: save the message as a file, upload it, and get the full transcript in any of more than 100 languages, as text you can check, edit and keep.

sections.h2: How to Convert Voicemail to Text

steps.h3: Save the voicemail as an audio file
steps.content: Share or save the message from your phone, or download it from your voicemail email. The next section shows where to find the file for iPhone, Android, Google Voice and work phone systems.
Upload the file from your phone or computer, or from Google Drive, Dropbox or OneDrive. It works the same in a mobile browser as on desktop.
TranscriptX detects the language on its own and writes out the whole voicemail as punctuated text. Turn timestamps on if you want to see when each part was said.
Check names and numbers against the audio, fix anything in place, then copy the text or download it as TXT, DOCX or PDF to keep a record.

sections.h2: How to Save a Voicemail as an Audio File
intro: TranscriptX doesn't connect to your voicemail box, so the first step is getting the message out as a file. Where it lives depends on the phone or system that took the call:

items.content: Open the Phone app and go to your voicemails (the Voicemail tab, or Calls filtered to Voicemails in the newer layout). Tap the message, tap Share, and choose Save to Files, or send it to yourself by Mail or Messages. The saved file is usually an .m4a audio file. Sharing works for Visual Voicemail, which most iPhone carriers support.

items.h3: Android and Samsung voicemail to text
items.content: In Phone by Google, expand the voicemail to share its audio recording. On Samsung Galaxy phones, open the Voicemail or Visual Voicemail app, select the message and use Save, Forward or Share. Menu names vary by phone maker and carrier, and some Samsung phones save voicemail as AMR files.

Google Voice already transcribes voicemail, but Google notes those transcripts may be incorrect or missing. To get the audio, turn on Get voicemail via email in Google Voice settings, or export your voicemails with Google Takeout, then upload the recording to TranscriptX.

items.h3: Microsoft Teams, Webex and office phone systems
items.content: Many business systems email each voicemail with the recording attached. Webex Calling attaches a WAV file, and Teams voicemail emails typically include an MP3. Save the attachment and upload it to get a full transcript you can file or forward.

sections.h2: When Your Phone's Voicemail Transcription Falls Short
intro: Built-in transcription is convenient, but these are the problems people run into most often, and where a full transcript of the saved file helps:

items.content: iPhone users regularly report on Apple's Community forums that a voicemail transcript shows only part of a message, sometimes just the last few seconds. Uploading the saved audio gives you every word, with timestamps.
Built-in transcription depends on your carrier, region, phone language and software version, so some messages never get a transcript. A saved voicemail file can still be transcribed in full.

items.h3: The voicemail isn't in a supported language
items.content: Phone by Google transcribes voicemail only in English and Spanish, and Live Voicemail covers a limited set of languages. A message in Vietnamese, Hindi or Arabic often comes back with no text at all.

Apple notes that voicemails not stored in iCloud can be erased by your carrier, and may be deleted when you change your SIM card. Saving the audio and a written copy keeps the message after it is gone from your phone.

content: A voicemail in a language you don't read well is the hardest kind to deal with, and built-in phone transcription usually can't help, because it doesn't support most languages in the first place.

TranscriptX first transcribes the voicemail in the language it was spoken, across more than 100 languages. You can then translate the transcript into English, so a Spanish, French, Vietnamese or Hindi voicemail becomes a message you can read in English. Translation is basic for now: fuller translation between more languages is coming soon.
Keep the original-language transcript next to the translation. For anything important, like an address, an amount or an appointment time, it's the original words that count.

sections.h2: Free Voicemail to Text Converter Online
content: TranscriptX is a free voicemail to text converter that works online, in any browser. You can try it without an account. Sign in to keep your transcripts saved on every device.

There is no per-message fee and no carrier add-on to subscribe to just to read a voicemail. Upload the file, read the text, and copy or download it. If you transcribe long or noisy recordings every day, the Pro plan adds more daily usage, bigger files, speaker labels and noise reduction.
A voicemail is easy to lose. Messages expire, phones get replaced, and voicemail boxes fill up. Voicemail transcription turns the message into a document you control.

When you transcribe voicemail to text with TranscriptX, you get a full voicemail transcript rather than a short preview. Download it as TXT, DOCX or PDF and file it with the job, the customer, the tenancy or the case it belongs to. Keep timestamps on to show exactly where in the message something was said, or turn them off for a clean block of text.

Because the voicemail to text transcription is plain text, you can search it later for a name, a date or an order number. Keep the original audio file alongside it, so the recording is there if anyone ever needs to hear it.

Voicemail is recorded over a phone line, so the audio is compressed and narrower than a normal recording, and callers are often outdoors, driving or rushing. A clear message from a quiet room comes back close to word for word. Wind, traffic, a weak signal or someone speaking fast can blur a word or two. For noisy messages, noise reduction on the Pro plan helps clean up the audio before it is transcribed.

The details that matter most in a voicemail are also the easiest to get wrong: phone numbers, street addresses, names, amounts and dates. Before you call back or act on a message, check those against the audio. With timestamps on, you can jump straight to the moment a number was said and listen to just that part.
TranscriptX detects the language automatically across more than 100 languages, so a voicemail in Spanish, French, Vietnamese or Hindi is transcribed without changing any settings first.
Not every spoken message arrives as voicemail. Voice messages in chat and messaging apps carry the same kind of information, and they are just as hard to skim.

Most messaging apps let you save or share a voice message as an audio file. Upload it to TranscriptX to transcribe the voice message to text, in the same way as a voicemail. Voice message transcription is handy when you can't play audio out loud, when a message is long, or when it's in a language you read more easily than you hear.

sections.h2: Do You Need a Voicemail to Text App?
content: Often, no. If your phone and carrier support it, the voicemail transcription built into iPhone, Phone by Google or Google Voice is the fastest way to glance at new messages, and it costs nothing. Use it.

TranscriptX is for the moments it can't help: a transcript that is cut off or missing, a voicemail in a language your phone doesn't transcribe, an old message you saved, a voicemail forwarded by a colleague, or a message you need to keep as a document. It runs in the browser, so it works like a voicemail to text app without the install, and as an alternative to an iPhone or Android voicemail to text app.
When people look for the best voicemail to text app, what usually matters is the whole message, in their language, in a form they can keep. That is the job TranscriptX is built for.

sections.h2: Privacy: What Happens to Your Voicemail
content: Voicemail can be personal, so it helps to know where it goes. Built-in services handle it differently: Google, for example, says Phone app voicemail transcripts are stored on your phone rather than in your Google Account, and that voicemails you choose to donate may be reviewed by people.

With TranscriptX, nothing is pulled from your voicemail box. You choose which saved file to upload. You can try it without an account, and if you sign in you can delete all your data from the account menu at any time.
